plants.scientific_name: Celosia cristata (Celosia argentea Cristata Group) 'Dracula Red'
plants.location: On the black crate by the porch post
plants.container: 8 in nursery pot (4 qt / 3.78 L) from the grower
plants.id_basis: The grower's tag reads 'Celosia Dracula Red, Celosia cristata'. The velvety, brain-like burgundy crests and bronze-tinged leaves match.
plants.id_alternatives: None needed; the tag confirms it
plants.temp_notes: A warm-season annual. Growth stalls below about 55 F, leaves and crests darken and spoil below about 45 F, and frost kills it. The tag says 'summer to frost'.
plants.humidity_notes: Fine in Texas humidity. Wet crests in long rainy spells can rot.
plants.light_notes: Full sun keeps the crests large and the colour deep. In shade the stems stretch and the crests stay small.
plants.winter_summary: Celosia is an annual: it finishes at the first frost. You can enjoy it until then, and save seed for next year.
plants.winter_triggers: No action needed; first frost ends it (about mid-November).
plants.winter_steps:
Enjoy it until the first frost; cover it with a sheet on a light-frost night to stretch the season a little.
To save seed: let a crest dry on the plant, cut it off, and rub it over paper; the tiny black seeds fall out. Store them dry and sow in April.
Cut a few crests now and hang them upside down somewhere dry: they keep their colour as dried flowers.
After frost, pull the plant and compost it (no disease seen).
plants.indoor_setup: Not worth bringing indoors; it needs strong sun and declines in winter light.
plants.health_summary: Three large, deep-red crests and full, healthy foliage with the bronze-purple tint typical of 'Dracula'.
plants.health_observations:
Large, unblemished crests
Leaves green with bronze-purple flushing (normal for this cultivar)
One yellowing leaf low on the plant
Some dry potting-mix debris on the tag
plants.health_steps:
Water at the base so the crests stay dry
Remove yellow leaves as they appear
Feed lightly every 2-3 weeks until early November, then stop
plants.notes: Grown by the same nursery as the petunia 'Ray Black' (matching tags, barcode 8 10224 33016 2). The two earlier celosias (Kelos Fire Purple and Glorious Orange) are plume types; this one is the crested type.
plants.pests_current: No pests seen in the photos.
plants.water_notes: Water when the top inch of mix is dry. Annuals in pots dry out quickly in heat; check daily in summer.
plants.soil_medium: Well-draining potting mix with a handful of compost.
plants.nutrients: Feed every 2-3 weeks while it blooms. Too much nitrogen gives leaves instead of flowers. Cosmos does best with very little food.
plants.pests_watch:
Aphids on buds and soft growth
Spider mites in hot, dry spells
Powdery mildew
Stem rot or damping-off in wet mix
Caterpillars
plants.pest_steps:
Look under leaves and at growing tips once a week.
Knock aphids and mites off with a strong spray of water in the morning.
Use insecticidal soap or neem oil in the evening for stubborn cases, every 5-7 days.
Pick off caterpillars by hand, or use Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis).
For mildew, remove the worst leaves, water at the base and give the plant airflow.

plants.location: On the black crate by the porch post
plants.container: 8 in nursery pot (4 qt / 3.78 L) from the grower
plants.id_basis: The tag from Spring Creek Growers (Waller, TX) reads 'Petunia Ray Black, Petunia hybrida', and the velvety near-black trumpets with lime-green, sticky-haired foliage match.
plants.id_alternatives: None needed; the tag confirms it
plants.temp_notes: Petunias handle Central Texas cool seasons well and take a light frost; damage starts around 28-30 F and a hard freeze in the low 20s kills them. Heat above about 95 F slows flowering.
plants.humidity_notes: Fine across a wide range. Flowers spot in long rainy spells.
plants.light_notes: More sun means more flowers. The tag says full to part sun; in the Texas summer, afternoon shade helps.
plants.winter_summary: Petunias often keep blooming through a mild Round Rock winter. Cover it on frost nights and it may carry on until spring.
plants.winter_triggers: Cover at 30 F; bring under the porch roof or into the garage below 26 F.
plants.winter_steps:
Cover at 30 F or below (frost cloth/sheet draped to the ground over a frame; frost cloth buys roughly 6-8 F). Bring in or move into the garage at 26 F or in a multi-day freeze.
Water the day before a freeze (moist soil holds heat) but keep the plant dry the rest of winter; skip watering when it is below 40 F.
Cluster pots against a south/east wall under the roof, away from north wind, and pile mulch or leaves around the pots.
Stop nitrogen fertilizer now; new tender growth freezes first.
Trim leggy stems back by a third in late November to keep it compact.
Water only when the top inch is dry; cool, wet mix rots the roots.
plants.indoor_setup: Not usually brought indoors. If you want to keep it, a sunny unheated garage window works better than a warm living room.
plants.health_summary: Vigorous and bushy with many buds and dark flowers. The foliage is quite light lime-green, which in petunias often means the plant is short of iron.
plants.health_observations:
Many velvety near-black flowers and buds
Light lime-green leaves overall (petunias show iron shortage early)
Some spent, twisted flowers
Sticky glandular hairs on stems (normal)
plants.health_steps:
Feed with a fertilizer that includes iron (a petunia or 'acid' bloom food) every 2 weeks while it blooms
If new leaves stay pale, give a dose of chelated iron
Pinch off spent flowers and their seed pods to keep it blooming
Pinch back long stems to keep it full
plants.notes: Bought with the celosia 'Dracula Red' (same grower tag style). A third, blurry photo of the tag was not used.
plants.pests_current: No pests seen. Light, lime-green foliage noted (likely iron shortage, not a pest).
plants.water_notes: Water when the top inch of mix is dry. Annuals in pots dry out quickly in heat; check daily in summer.
plants.soil_medium: Well-draining potting mix with a handful of compost.
plants.fertilizer: Bloom fertilizer that includes iron (petunia or acid-loving plant food)
plants.nutrients: Petunias are hungry and very prone to iron shortage: pale, yellow-green new leaves with green veins. Feed every 1-2 weeks while blooming with a fertilizer that contains iron, and keep the pH on the acid side (5.5-6.2). Hard, alkaline tap water makes iron shortage worse; a chelated iron dose fixes it within a couple of weeks.
plants.pests_watch:
Aphids on buds and soft growth
Spider mites in hot, dry spells
Powdery mildew
Stem rot or damping-off in wet mix
Caterpillars
plants.pest_steps:
Look under leaves and at growing tips once a week.
Knock aphids and mites off with a strong spray of water in the morning.
Use insecticidal soap or neem oil in the evening for stubborn cases, every 5-7 days.
Pick off caterpillars by hand, or use Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis).
For mildew, remove the worst leaves, water at the base and give the plant airflow.

plants.aliases: White sagebrush; Louisiana sagewort; Prairie sage; Silver sage
plants.location: On the black crate by the porch post
plants.id_basis: The H-E-B Texas Roots tag reads 'White Sage, Artemisia ludoviciana', and the narrow, silver-felted, aromatic leaves fit. This is not the Californian white sage used for smudging (Salvia apiana); it is a different plant that happens to share the common name.
plants.id_alternatives: None needed; the tag confirms it
plants.temp_notes: Very cold-hardy (to about -30 F) and heat-tolerant. Cold is no concern in Round Rock; winter wet is the only thing that harms it.
plants.humidity_notes: Prefers dry air. Humid, still weather can bring mildew; give it airflow.
plants.light_notes: Full sun keeps it compact and silver. In shade it gets floppy and greener.
plants.winter_summary: Fully hardy. It may die back to the ground or look ragged in winter and regrows in spring.
plants.winter_steps:
Leave it outside all winter.
Keep the pot off saucers so it never sits in water; winter wet is the risk, not cold.
Cut it back to a few inches in late February to get fresh silver growth.
Plant it in the ground in fall or spring if you like; see the note about spreading.
plants.health_summary: Bright silver, healthy young foliage with no spots or pests. A little stretched, which is normal for nursery stock.
plants.health_observations:
Healthy silver, felted leaves
Slightly leggy stems
Gritty, fast-draining nursery mix
plants.health_steps:
Give it full sun
Pinch the tips once to make it bushier
Water only when the top 2 in is dry
plants.notes: Spreads strongly by underground runners once in the ground; give it room or plant it where spreading is welcome (or keep it in a pot). Leaves are aromatic but this Artemisia is bitter and not a culinary herb.
plants.pests_current: No pests seen in the photos.
plants.water_notes: In a pot, water when the top 2 in of mix is dry: about twice a week in summer heat, every 1-2 weeks in cool weather, and only in dry spells in winter. Once planted in the ground and established, it needs watering only in long droughts.
plants.soil_medium: Lean, fast-draining soil. In a pot: potting mix with 30% decomposed granite, pumice or coarse sand. In the ground: native soil is fine; do not add rich compost.
plants.fertilizer: None, or a light slow-release feed once in spring
plants.nutrients: Texas natives grow best in lean soil. Rich feeding gives floppy, weak growth and fewer flowers. One light feeding in spring is plenty; skip it entirely once planted in the ground.
plants.pests_watch:
Powdery mildew in humid, still weather
Aphids on soft new growth
Root rot if the mix stays wet in winter
Spider mites in hot, dry spells
plants.pest_steps:
Look under leaves and at growing tips once a week.
Knock aphids and mites off with a strong spray of water in the morning.
Use insecticidal soap or neem oil in the evening for stubborn cases, every 5-7 days.
Pick off caterpillars by hand, or use Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis).
For mildew, remove the worst leaves, water at the base and give the plant airflow.

Cut the old stems to about 2 in once they have browned (December to February).

plants.location: On the concrete by the steps

plants.temp_notes: Heat- and drought-tough. Hard freezes kill the top back; the roots survive to about 10 F in the ground and it regrows in spring. Roots in a pot are more exposed.
plants.light_notes: Full sun for the most flowers; it tolerates part shade but blooms less.
plants.winter_summary: Evergreen in mild winters, freezes back in hard ones and regrows from the base.
plants.winter_triggers: Mulch or group the pot on nights below 25 F; it stays outside.
plants.winter_steps:
Leave it outside.
On nights forecast below 25 F, push the pot against the house wall with the others and mulch over the soil.
Cut it back by half in late February to keep it compact.
Planting in the ground (fall is ideal) makes it much tougher than in a pot.
plants.health_summary: A young plant with a fresh flower and new buds. Sparse and a bit leggy, as most 1 gal natives are at this age.

Healthy green, rough leaves
plants.health_steps:

plants.aliases: Scarlet rose mallow; Scarlet swamp hibiscus; Texas star
plants.location: On the concrete by the steps
plants.container: 1 gal H-E-B Texas Roots 'Natives' pot, with a wire hook in the soil
plants.id_basis: The H-E-B Texas Roots tag reads 'Texas Star Hibiscus, Hibiscus coccineus', and the deeply cut, finger-like (palmate) leaves with red leaf stalks fit. Its big red star-shaped flowers come in summer.
plants.id_alternatives: None needed; the tag confirms it
plants.id_improve: A flower photo next summer, just for the record
plants.temp_notes: Hardy perennial: the stems die to the ground after frost and new shoots come up in spring. Cold-hardy to about -10 F in the ground; protect a potted one from hard freezes.
plants.humidity_notes: Loves humidity; it grows wild in swamps and ditches.
plants.light_notes: Full sun for flowering. It takes part shade but blooms less.
plants.winter_summary: It goes dormant: the leaves drop and the stems die back after frost. The roots regrow in spring, often late (May), so do not give up on it.
plants.winter_triggers: Mulch the pot on nights below 25 F.
plants.winter_steps:
Let it go dormant outside.
When the stems are brown and dry, cut them to about 6 in. Mark the pot so you remember it is alive.
Keep the mix slightly moist all winter; unlike most plants it should not dry out completely.
Mulch or wrap the pot in a hard freeze below 20 F.
plants.health_summary: Upright and growing, but many leaves have ragged holes and notches from chewing insects, and a few lower leaves are yellowing.
plants.health_observations:
Holes and notched leaf edges on many leaves (chewing insects: hibiscus sawfly larvae, grasshoppers or caterpillars)
A couple of yellowing lower leaves
Red leaf stalks and stems (normal)
Tall single stem in a small pot
plants.health_steps:
Look under the leaves, especially in the morning, for small green worm-like larvae (hibiscus sawfly). Pick them off or spray insecticidal soap; spinosad also works
Remove badly chewed leaves
Keep it well watered; it likes moist soil
Plant it in the ground or a large pot in a sunny, damp spot
plants.notes: Unusual among natives: it wants moist soil and does well near a downspout or in a rain garden.
plants.pests_current: Chewing damage on many leaves (holes and notches). The insect itself is not visible; hibiscus sawfly larvae are the usual cause on this plant.
plants.water_notes: Keep the soil moist; it is a wetland plant. In a pot in summer that can mean daily watering. Water less in winter dormancy, but do not let it dry out completely.
plants.soil_medium: Rich, moisture-holding soil with compost. It tolerates clay and wet spots.
plants.nutrients: Feed every 3-4 weeks from April to August with a balanced fertilizer. It grows tall and fast in rich, moist soil. Stop feeding in late summer so it can go dormant.
plants.pests_watch:
Hibiscus sawfly larvae (small green 'worms' that skeletonise leaves)
Grasshoppers and caterpillars
Aphids and whiteflies on new growth
Spider mites in dry heat
plants.pest_steps:
Look under leaves and at growing tips once a week.
Knock aphids and mites off with a strong spray of water in the morning.
Use insecticidal soap or neem oil in the evening for stubborn cases, every 5-7 days.
Pick off caterpillars by hand, or use Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis).
For mildew, remove the worst leaves, water at the base and give the plant airflow.

plants.location: Wire rack by the fence, with the other roses
plants.container: Burgundy-red plastic pot with a bark, perlite and pumice mix
plants.id_basis: Compound leaves with serrated leaflets, small double flowers and a compact habit make this a miniature rose. One clear yellow bloom is open. This is the 'second rose in the red pot' from the to-photograph list.
plants.id_alternatives: A small patio or polyantha rose (less likely given the size)
plants.id_improve: The plant tag or receipt for the cultivar name (optional)
plants.temp_notes: Hardy; it goes semi-dormant in winter. In a pot the roots are exposed, so group and mulch the pot in hard freezes.
plants.humidity_notes: Humid, wet weather raises black spot and mildew pressure.
plants.light_notes: Needs full sun to bloom; afternoon shade in midsummer helps a small pot.
plants.winter_summary: Hardy outdoors in Round Rock. Keep it outside, group the pot with the other roses and prune in late February.
plants.winter_triggers: Mulch and group the pots on nights below 20 F.
plants.winter_steps:
Stop feeding by early November.
Group the rose pots against a wall and mulch the soil surface on nights below 20 F.
Remove dead twigs now; leave the main pruning for late February.
Water when the top inch is dry; less in winter.
plants.health_summary: Leafy, green and flowering, but several spent blooms have dried on the plant and a few twigs have died back.
plants.health_observations:
One fresh yellow bloom
Several dried, brown spent blooms
A few dead brown twigs at the base
A couple of yellowing leaflets
Healthy bright green new leaves
plants.health_steps:
Deadhead: cut each spent bloom back to the first leaf with five leaflets
Cut dead twigs back to green, healthy wood
Water deeply when the top inch is dry
Remove any leaves with black spots
plants.notes: One of four potted roses on the rack (see the other rose records). Weeds (spotted spurge) are growing in the neighbouring pots.
plants.pests_current: No pests seen in the photos.
plants.water_notes: Water deeply 1-2 times a week, more in summer heat. Water at the base, not over the leaves. In winter, water only when the mix is dry and the weather is above freezing.
plants.soil_medium: Rich loam or potting mix with compost, mulched with 2 in of bark.
plants.nutrients: Feed after the late-winter pruning (February), then every 4-6 weeks until September. Stop feeding 6 weeks before the first frost. Yellowing between veins can be iron or magnesium.
plants.pests_watch:
Black spot and powdery mildew
Aphids and spider mites
Rose rosette virus (a Texas risk: witches' broom, red bristly growth)
Japanese beetles and cane borers
plants.pest_steps:
Water at the base and give the plant airflow.
Remove and bin leaves with black spot; do not compost them.
Rinse off aphids and mites with water; use soap or neem for stubborn cases.
If you see rosette (red, bristly, distorted shoots), cut the plant out and bin it.

Indoor winter air is typically 20-35% RH; raise it with a humidifier (target 50-60%), grouping plants, or a pebble tray, and keep plants away from heater vents.

Root rot from cold, soggy mix

plants.pest_steps:
Check leaf undersides and leaf joints once a week, and before any plant comes indoors.
Keep newly moved plants apart from the others for 2 weeks.
Wipe leaves with a damp cloth to remove dust and mites.

Water the day before a freeze (moist soil holds heat) but keep the plant dry the rest of winter; skip watering when it is below 40 F.
Cluster pots against a south/east wall under the roof, away from north wind, and pile mulch or leaves around the pots.
Stop nitrogen fertilizer now; new tender growth freezes first.
